q: The pitch of the note (how high it is) is determined by its frequency.
e: True. Greater frequency, higher pitch. Amplitude sets loudness, not pitch. Pitch, how high the note is, is set by frequency.

q: The pitch of the note (how high it is) is determined by its amplitude.
e: False. Pitch is set by frequency, not amplitude. Larger amplitude makes a louder note. Higher frequency makes a higher note.

q: The greater the frequency, the higher is the pitch.
e: True. Pitch is how high the note sounds, and frequency sets it. Raise frequency and pitch rises. Amplitude changes loudness, not high-or-low character.

q: The loudness of the note depends upon the amplitude of the wave that produces it.
e: True. Intensity is proportional to A squared, and is the objective W m^-2 measure. Loudness itself is a subjective sensation. Loudness depends on amplitude: bigger A, more energy, louder note.

q: The greater the amplitude, the louder the note, because more energy is used to produce a larger amplitude.
e: True. greater and amplitude have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of greater would describe a different law.

q: The greater the amplitude, the softer the note, because less energy is used to produce a larger amplitude.
e: False. Larger amplitude means a louder note, because more energy went into the wave. Softer would be a smaller amplitude. Energy and loudness rise together with A.

q: Quality of a sound is the characteristic which distinguishes the two sounds of the same loudness and same pitch but emitted by two different instruments.
e: True. It usually grows with intensity, which itself grows with amplitude squared. Two listeners can disagree, so loudness is subjective. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium.

q: The notes produced by the violin is richer than others because it has more overtones.
e: True. A different driver in place of notes would describe a different law. notes and produced have to stay with the same process.

q: Notes of the same pitch played upon different musical instruments are distinguished from each other by their quality.
e: True. Amplitude changes loudness, not high-or-low character. Pitch is how high the note sounds, and frequency sets it. Raise frequency and pitch rises.

q: The timbre of a sound depends on its waveform, which varies with the number of overtones or harmonics.
e: True. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum. Timbre, or quality, lets you tell instruments apart at the same pitch and loudness.

q: The intensity of the sound at a place is the energy transmitted per second per unit area held normally to direction of sound.
e: True. Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, not to amplitude itself. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum.

q: The intensity of a wave is directly proportional to the amplitude of the wave.
e: False. Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, not to amplitude itself. Double A and I becomes four times. That is why I carries A^2 in I = (1/2) rho v omega^2 A^2.

q: Loudness is a sensation and hence, unlike intensity, it depends on the observer.
e: True. Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, not to amplitude itself. Loudness is the ear's sensation of a sound. It usually grows with intensity, which itself grows with amplitude squared.

q: To the human ears, the loudness of the sound is subjective.
e: True. Two listeners can disagree, so loudness is subjective. Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a compressible medium. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum.

q: To the human ears, the loudness of the sound is objective.
e: False. Loudness is a sensation, so to human ears it is subjective. Intensity is the objective watt-per-square-metre measure. Two listeners can disagree on loudness at the same intensity.

q: Normally the greater the intensity, the greater the loudness of the sound is.
e: True. It is not electromagnetic, so it cannot cross vacuum. Stiffer media generally carry it faster. Sound intensity is power per unit area, in W m^-2.
